title: When a Precedent Loses Its Foundation
hook: A 1980 ruling barred the Ten Commandments from public classrooms. An appeals court says the test it rested on is gone — so the ruling is too. That claim is now at the Supreme Court.
key_points: Texas S.B. 10 (2025) requires a Ten Commandments display in every public school classroom, using King James Bible text.
Stone v. Graham (1980) struck down a nearly identical Kentucky law under the Establishment Clause.
Stone applied the Lemon test; Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022) replaced Lemon with an inquiry into history and tradition.
The 5th Circuit upheld the Texas law 9-8 in April 2026: 'With Lemon extracted, there is nothing left of Stone.'
Texas families, represented by the ACLU, asked the Supreme Court to take the case on August 17, 2026.
content_html: The Establishment Clause bars government from establishing religion, but the hard question has always been what counts. For decades courts answered it with the Lemon test, a three-part inquiry into a law's purpose, effect, and entanglement with religion. In 1980, Stone v. Graham used that framework to strike down a Kentucky law requiring the Ten Commandments in every public classroom. In 2022, Kennedy v. Bremerton set Lemon aside in favor of looking at historical practice — and that raised a question nobody had to answer before: what happens to the rulings Lemon produced?
extra_html: SCOTUSblog's Amy Howe reports the collision. Texas enacted S.B. 10 in 2025, requiring a King James Bible text of the Ten Commandments to hang in every public elementary and secondary classroom — a law close enough to Kentucky's that Stone would seem to settle it. In April 2026 the full 5th Circuit upheld it anyway by a single vote, 9-8, reasoning that Stone was only ever an application of Lemon: "With Lemon extracted, there is nothing left of Stone." On August 17, 2026, Texas families represented by the ACLU asked the Supreme Court to take the case. The dispute is a clean illustration of how doctrine actually changes. Precedents are rarely repealed outright; more often the framework beneath them is replaced, and lower courts are left to argue about how much of the old building is still standing — with the Supreme Court as the only body that can say for certain.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 5th Circuit's argument for upholding the Texas classroom display law?
flashcards.back_html: That Stone v. Graham (1980) rested on the Lemon test, and once the Supreme Court abandoned Lemon in Kennedy v. Bremerton, the older ruling had no foundation left: "With Lemon extracted, there is nothing left of Stone."

flashcards.prompt: What changed in Establishment Clause analysis after Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022)?

choices.text: Courts look to historical practice and tradition instead of applying the Lemon test
The Establishment Clause was held to apply only to Congress
Religious displays became mandatory in public buildings

flashcards.explanation_html: Kennedy shifted the inquiry toward the historical understanding of the clause, displacing Lemon's three-part framework.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a lower court declaring an old precedent hollowed-out constitutionally awkward?

choices.text: Only the Supreme Court can overrule its own decisions, so a 9-8 appeals ruling invites review
Appeals courts may never cite Supreme Court cases

flashcards.explanation_html: A lower court treating a precedent as defunct rather than distinguished is exactly the kind of conflict the Supreme Court steps in to resolve.
